questions.question_text: Determine whether the curve $f(x) = 3x^2 - 12x + 5$ is increasing, decreasing, or stationary at $x = 1$.

options.why: Mistook the positive leading coefficient of the quadratic for an increasing gradient at the point.
Confused evaluating the derivative at $x = 1$ with setting the derivative equal to zero.
Evaluated $f'(1) = -6 < 0$ and confused a negative first derivative (decreasing) with negative concavity (concave down).

questions.solution_text:
$f'(x) = 6x - 12$
$f'(1) = 6(1) - 12 = -6$
Since $f'(1) < 0$, the function is decreasing at $x = 1$.

questions.question_text: For what values of $x$ is $f(x) = 2x^2 - 12x + 9$ increasing?

options.why: Reversed the inequality sign for an increasing function.
Forgot to divide by 4 when solving the linear inequality.
Reversed the inequality and made an arithmetic error in division.

questions.solution_text:
$f'(x) = 4x - 12$
For the function to be increasing, $f'(x) > 0$:
$4x - 12 > 0$
$4x > 12$
$x > 3$

questions.question_text: For what values of $x$ is $f(x) = 15 + 8x - 2x^2$ decreasing?

options.why: Forgot that dividing by a negative number reverses the inequality.
Differentiated 2x squared as 2x instead of 4x.
Applied negative signs incorrectly when rearranging the inequality.

questions.solution_text:
$f'(x) = 8 - 4x$
For the function to be decreasing, $f'(x) < 0$:
$8 - 4x < 0$
$-4x < -8$
$x > 2$

questions.question_text: For what values of $x$ is $f(x) = x^3 - 12x + 4$ increasing?

options.why: Found the interval where the function is decreasing instead of increasing.
Omitted the left-hand interval where the quadratic derivative is also positive.
Treated the quadratic inequality as a single linear inequality.

questions.solution_text:
$f'(x) = 3x^2 - 12$
For the function to be increasing, $f'(x) > 0$:
$3(x^2 - 4) > 0$
$3(x - 2)(x + 2) > 0$
$x < -2 \text{ or } x > 2$

questions.question_text: For what values of $x$ is $f(x) = 2x^3 - 3x^2 - 36x + 10$ decreasing?

options.why: Found the region where the cubic is increasing rather than decreasing.
Swapped the signs of the roots of the quadratic derivative.
Ignored the lower root boundary when solving the quadratic inequality.

questions.solution_text:
$f'(x) = 6x^2 - 6x - 36$
For the function to be decreasing, $f'(x) < 0$:
$6(x^2 - x - 6) < 0$
$6(x - 3)(x + 2) < 0$
$-2 < x < 3$

questions.question_text: Which statement correctly explains why $f(x) = 2x^3 + 6x + 1$ is increasing for all real values of $x$?

options.text: $f'(x) = 6x^2 + 6 = 0$ has real roots where the gradient stays positive.
options.why: Incorrectly claimed that 6x^2 + 6 = 0 has real roots when it has none.

options.text: $f(0) = 1 > 0$, so the function is positive and therefore increasing everywhere.
options.why: Confused a positive y-intercept with the function being increasing everywhere.

options.text: $f'(x) = 6x^2 + 6x$, which is non-negative for all positive values of x.
options.why: Differentiated 6x as 6x instead of the constant derivative 6.

questions.solution_text:
$f'(x) = 6x^2 + 6$
$= 6(x^2 + 1)$
Since $x^2 \geq 0$ for all real $x$, $6(x^2 + 1) \geq 6 > 0$.
Since $f'(x) > 0$ for all real $x$, $f(x)$ is increasing for all $x$.

questions.question_text: Find the values of $x$ for which $f(x) = 3x^2 - 2x^3$ is increasing.

options.why: Found the outer regions where the negative quadratic derivative is negative.
Differentiated 3x squared as 2x instead of 6x.
Only checked the upper root without solving the full quadratic inequality.

questions.solution_text:
$f'(x) = 6x - 6x^2$
For the function to be increasing, $f'(x) > 0$:
$6x(1 - x) > 0$
$0 < x < 1$

questions.question_text: For what values of $k$ is $f'(x) > 0$ for all real $x$ for the cubic $f(x) = x^3 - 6x^2 + kx - 1$?

options.why: Reversed the inequality when moving $-12k$ across, writing $k < 12$ instead of $12k > 144$.
Left the leading coefficient $3$ out of $4ac$, using $\Delta = 144 - 4k < 0$ and getting $k > 36$.
Made both slips: dropped the $3$ from $4ac$ and then reversed the inequality, turning $144 - 4k < 0$ into $k < 36$.

questions.solution_text:
$f'(x) = 3x^2 - 12x + k$
For $f'(x) > 0$ for all real $x$, the quadratic must have positive leading coefficient and negative discriminant.
Since the leading coefficient $3 > 0$, we require $\Delta < 0$:
$\Delta = (-12)^2 - 4(3)(k) < 0$
$144 - 12k < 0$
$12k > 144$
$k > 12$
